newsitem.title: USA: Bankers tout appeal of Latin project finance.
newsitem.headline: Bankers tout appeal of Latin project finance.

text.p: The market for large-scale project financing in Latin America has rebounded from financial setbacks associated with the Mexican peso crisis two years ago and is set for strong growth, investment bankers said Friday.
"Things are looking up for the region," Craig Falkenhagen, managing director of Bank of America's Global Project Finance Group told a Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade conference here.
Bank of America is a unit of BankAmerica Corp.

He said economic growth for the Latin American region is expected to be three percent this year and four to six percent per year thereafter, and cited research showing that Latin America will need $150 billion in infrastructure projects in the next 15 years. "The numbers are huge," he said.

In the past few years, Latin American project financings have taken off, after a period of relative inactivity following the region's 1982 debt crisis, noted Michael Clayton, vice president at Citicorp Securities Inc, a unit of Citicorp.
"The market is emerging from a long period of inactivity," he said, noting that there have been 10 to 12 major project financing deals in each of the last two years.
"Many of the countries now face a period of catchup for a lost period of investment," Clayton said.

Falkenhagen listed recent projects along the lines of Mexico's $647 million Samalayuca II power project, and said new projects include a gas pipeline from Brazil to Bolivia, a pipeline to bring gas from Argentina into Santiago and Brazil's B Band cellular telecommunications project.
The bankers said the leading countries for project financing were Chile, Colombia, Brazil, Argentina and Mexico.
And they said the principal industries for investment were telecommunications, power, oil and gas, metals and mining. Clayton said Citicorp did not see much activity in infrastructure.
Clayton said that, of 50 financings in the last decade or so he knew of no writeoffs and just two that needed to be restructured.

But the bankers acknowledged that there will be difficulty finding the amount of funding that will be needed in the international commercial market, and said local currency markets would have to pick up the slack.

Clayton said there is a broader variety of banks involved in Latin American project financing, but that European banks account for the majority, with U.S. involvement typically limited to the five or so large "money center" banks. "Super-regionals and regionals have shown very little interest," he said. He said Japanese banks were very active.

Project financing in Latin America is attractive, he said, because yields are much higher, the credit structure tends to be more conservative, political risks are mitigated through insurance and there has been a low rate of credit writeoff.
